title: Napkin math
subtitle: Turn a product idea into servers, storage and bandwidth, with math that fits on a napkin.

steps.title: Is one server enough?
steps.text:
A photo app with **10 million** users a day. Before choosing a database or a framework,
answer one question: is this one machine, or a hundred?

callout.text: You need the right order of magnitude

card.title: The brief
lines: 1M photo uploads a day, 2 MB each

steps.title: Users → requests per second
steps.text:
10M users × 20 requests = **200M requests a day**.
A day has 86,400 seconds. Round it to **100,000**: napkin math is about speed.

callout.text: Handy shortcut: 1M requests a day ≈ 12 per second.

steps.title: Plan for the busiest hour
steps.text: Traffic is not flat. Evenings and big events run about **3×** the daily average.

callout.text: A system sized for the average goes down exactly when most people show up.

steps.title: How many servers?
steps.text:
A load test shows one server handles about **1,000 req/s**.
7,000 ÷ 1,000 = 7, plus room for a failure and spikes: **10 servers**.
changes: + Web tier (4 drawn, 10 in real life)

steps.title: How much storage?
steps.text:
1M photos × 2 MB = **2 TB a day**, about **730 TB a year**.
Keep 3 copies so a dead disk loses nothing: plan for **~2 PB**.

callout.text: Requests come and go. Bytes stay

steps.title: The real limit is bandwidth
steps.text:
Each user views ~100 thumbnails of 200 KB: **200 TB a day going out**, about **16 Gbit/s**.
That is a job for a CDN, not for ten web servers.

callout.text: Read-heavy media apps run out of bandwidth before they run out of CPU.

changes: ~ Web tier only serves the app

steps.title: What we learned
steps.text:
- **Users × actions ÷ 100,000** gives requests per second.
- Multiply by **3** for the peak, and size for that.
- **Servers** = peak ÷ one server's measured capacity, plus headroom.
- **Storage** = items a day × size × 365 × copies.
- Always estimate **bytes out** too.

callout.text: Next idea: spreading those 7,000 requests over 10 servers is the load balancer's job.
